senses: on the other hand, on the contrary, whereas
la:conj:autem.html:
autem,
conj. [v. aut init.], on the other hand, but, yet, however, nevertheless; sometimes an emphasized and (it is never found at the beginning of a clause, but after one or more words; v. fin.; like at, it joins to a preceding thought a new one, either entirely antithetical or simply different; it differs from the restricting sed in like manner with at; v. at init., and cf.: [Popilius imperator tenebat provinciam; in cujus exercitu Catonis filius tiro militabat. Cum autem Popilio videretur unam dimittere legionem, Catonis quoque filium ... dimisit. Sed cum amore pugnandi in exercitu permansisset, Cato ad Popilium scripsit, etc.], B. and K. (most freq. in philos. lang.; rare in the histt., being used by Caes. only 59 times, by Sall. 23, and by Tac. 31; and very rare in the poets).
In joining an entirely antithetical thought, on the contrary, but = at quidem, at vero, δὲ δή, esp. freq. with the pronouns ego, tu, ille, qui, etc.: Ait se obligāsse crus fractum Aesculapio, Apollini autem bracchium,: Nam injusta ab justis impetrari non decet, Justa autem ab injustis petere insipientiast,: ego hic cesso, quia ipse nihil scribo: lego autem libentissime,; ; Plaut. Men. 2, 1, 43: i sane cum illo, Phrygia; tu autem, Eleusium, Huc intro abi ad nos,; ; ; ; ; : mihi ad enarrandum hoc argumentumst comitas, Si ad auscultandum vostra erit benignitas. Qui autem auscultare nolit, exsurgat foras,; so ; : Quid tu aïs, Gnatho? Numquid habes quod contemnas? Quid tu autem, Thraso?: e principio oriuntur omnia; ipsum autem nullā ex re aliā nasci potest,.—
In joining a thought that is simply different.
In gen., on the other hand, but, moreover.
Absol., as the Gr. δέ: Vehit hic clitellas, vehit hic autem alter senex,: cum Speusippum, sororis filium, Plato philosophiae quasi heredem reliquisset, duo autem praestantissimos studio atque doctrinā, Xenocratem Chalcedonium et Aristotelem Stagiritem, etc.,; : Alexandrum consultum, cui relinqueret regnum, voluisse optimum deligi, judicatum autem ab ipso optimum Perdiccam, cui anulum tradidisset,: Atque haec in moribus. De benevolentiā autem, quam etc.,; : Sed poëtae quid quemque deceat ex personā judicabunt; nobis autem personam imposuit natura etc.,; 1, 28, 98; 1, 43, 152: Quod semper movetur aeternum est; quod autem motum adfert alicui etc.,; sq.; 1, 30, 74; 1, 36, 87.—So sometimes when one conditional sentence is opposed to another, si—sin autem, in Gr. εἰ μέν— εἰ δέ: Nam si supremus ille dies non exstinctionem, sed commutationem adfert loci, quid optabilius? Sin autem etc.,; —In adducing an example of a rule: Et Demosthenes autem ad Aeschinem orationem in prooemio convertit, et M. Tullius etc., Spald.; also in passing from a particular to a general thought: Et sane plus habemus quam capimus. Insatiabilis autem avaritia est etc.,.—
Preceded by quidem, as in Gr. μέν—δέ (perh. most freq. in Cicero's philosophical works, under the influence of Greek style): Et haec quidem hoc modo; nihil autem melius extremo,: Sed nunc quidem valetudini tribuamus aliquid, cras autem etc.,; ; and thus in Tac. several times, but only in Ann. and Or.: bene intellegit ceteros quidem iis niti... Marcellum autem et Crispum attulisse etc., Or. 8; 18 bis; 25; A. 3, 53; 3, 73; 4, 28.—So often in transitions from one subject to another: Ac de inferendā quidem injuriā satis dictum est. Praetermittendae autem defensionis etc.,; ; .—So very often in Vulg. in direct reproduction of μέν—δέ: Ego quidem baptizo vos in aquā in paenitentiam; qui autem post me etc., Matt. 3, 11; 9, 37; 13, 23; 13, 32; 17, 11 sq.; 23, 28; 25, 33; 26, 24. —
Esp.
In any kind of transition: M. Antonius in eo libro, quem unum reliquit, disertos ait se vidisse multos, eloquentem omnino neminem. Vir autem acerrimo ingenio (sic enim fuit) multa etc.,: hic (pater) prout ipse amabat litteras, omnibus doctrinis, quibus puerilis aetas impertiri debet, filium erudivit: erat autem in puero summa suavitas oris,; also in questions: Quid autem magno opere Oppianicum metuebat, etc.,. Freq. several times repeated: Expetuntur autem divitiae cum ad usus vitae necessarios, tum ad perfruendas voluptates: in quibus autem major est animus, in iis pecuniae cupiditas spectat ad opes, etc., and 25; cf. Wopkens, Lectt. Tull. pp. 53 and 122: Orbis situm dicere adgredior... Dicam autem alias plura et exactius, Mel. prooem. 2.—
In repeating a word from a previous clause, in continuing a train of thought: admoneri me satis est: admonebit autem nemo alius nisi rei publicae tempus,: disces quam diu voles; tam diu autem velle debebis, quoad etc.,: nunc quod agitur, agamus: agitur autem, liberine vivamus an mortem obeamus,. —So esp. in impassioned discourse, Plant. Mil. 3, 1, 84: humanum amare est, humanum autem ignoscere est,; : quot potiones mulsi! quot autem prandia!; : quā pulchritudine urbem, quibus autem opibus praeditam, servitute oppressam tenuit civitatem,.—
Like sed, vero, igitur, etc., in resuming a train of thought interrupted by a parenthesis: Omnino illud honestum, quod ex animo excelso magnificoque quaerimus, animi efficitur non corporis viribus: exercendum tamen corpus et ita adficiendum est, ut oboedire consilio rationique possit in exsequendis negotiis et in labore tolerando: honestum autem id, quod exquirimus, totum est positum in animi curā, etc.,; .—
In introducing a parenthetical clause itself: quae autem nos ut recta aut recte facta dicamus, si placet (illi autem appellant κατορθώματα) omnes numeros virtutis continent, : quod vitium effugere qui volet (omnes autem velle debent) adhibebit etc.,; ; ; : In primis foedera ac leges (erant autem eae duodecim tabuiae et quaedam regiae leges) conquiri etc.,; : ex hoc Quodcumque est (minus est autem quam rhetoris aera) Discipuli custos praemordet,.—
In enumerations, for the purpose of adding an important circumstance: magnus dicendi labor, magna res, magna dignitas, summa autem gratia,but, and indeed,: animis omnes tenduntur insidiae... vel ab eā, quae penitus in omni sensu implicata insidet, imitatrix boni, voluptas, malorum autem mater omnium,yea, the parent of all evil,; : docet ratio mathematicorum, luna quantum absit a proxumā Mercurii stellā, multo autem longius a Veneris,.—
In the syllogism, to introduce the minor proposition (the assumptio or propositio minor; cf. atque, IV. 9., and atqui, II. D.), now, but; but now: Aut hoc, aut illud: hoc autem non, igitur illud. Itemque: aut hoc, aut illud: non autem hoc: illud igitur,: Si lucet, lucet: lucet autem, lucet igitur,: Si dicis te mentiri verumque dicis, mentiris: dicis autem te mentiri verumque dicis: mentiris igitur,; ; .—
Like the Gr. δέ or δή in adding an emphatic question (freq. in the comic poets), but, indeed.
In gen.: Quem te autem deum nominem?: Perii: quid hoc autemst mali?: Quī istuc? Quae res te sollicitat autem?: Quae autem divina? Vigere, sapere, invenire, meminisse,: Quo modo autem moveri animus ad appetendum potest, si id, quod videtur, non percipitur? πῶς δή, : Quo modo autem tibi placebit JOVEM LAPIDEM jurare, cum scias etc.,: Veni ad Caesarem: quis est autem Caesar?.—So in exclamations: Quantā delectatione autem adficerer, cum etc.,.—
In questions implying rebuke, reproach: Ba. Metuo credere. Ps. Credere autem? eho, etc., : Th. Ego non tangam meam? Ch. Tuam autem, furcifer? yours do you say? yours indeed! .—
In a question where a correction is made: Num quis testis Postumum appellavit? testis autem? (witness did I say?) num accusator? : Alio me vocat numerosa gloria tua: alio autem? quasi vero etc.,: Quid tandem isti mali in tam tenerā insulā non fecissent? non fecissent autem? imo quid ante adventum meum non fecerunt?; ; : Adimas etiam Hispanias? Et si inde cessero, in Africam transcendes. Transcendes autem dico? Weissenb.—
And in questions sed autem are sometimes both used, especially by the comic poets, but indeed, but now, like the Gr. ἀλλά — δέ (̓Αλλὰ ποῦ δὲ βούλει καθεζόμενοι ἀναγνῶμεν; .): Sed autem quid si hanc hinc apstulerit quispiam Sacram urnam Veneris?; and separated: Sed quid haec hic autem tam diu ante aedīs stetit?: Attat Phaedriae Pater venit. Sed quid pertimui autem, belua?: Sed quid ego haec autem nequiquam ingrata revolvo? * .—Once ast autem: ast autem tenui

quae candent lumine Phatnae, ap. P. (IV. 2, p. 555 Orell.).—

With interjections: Heia autem inimicos!: Ecce autem litigium,but lo!; so ; ; ; ; : Ecce autem alterum, Ruhnk.: Ecce autem subitum divortium,; so ; ; ; : Ecce autem aliud minus dubium,: Eccere autem capite nutat,; so : eccui autem non proditur [revertenti]?.!*? In good prose writers autem is usu. placed after the first word of a clause; but if several words, a subst. and prep., the verb esse with the predicate, a word with a negative, etc., together form one idea, then autem stands after the second or third word. But the poets, especially the comic poets, allow themselves greater liberty, and sometimes place this particle, without any necessity in the nature of the clause, in the third, fourth, or fifth place; but autem is never found in good writers at the beginning of a clause or sentence; cf. . See more upon this word in Hand, Turs. I. pp. 558-588.

senses: Introduces a correction to the previous words or an afterthought remark.
la:conj:aut.html:
aut,
conj. [aut, Osc. auti, Umbr. ote, ute, may be a modification of autem, as at of et, the suffix -t being a relic of the demonstrative -tem, which appears in item, and is the same as -dem in quidem, and -dam in quondam, and of which the demonstrative adverbs, tam and tum, are absolute forms; the first part of these words may be compared with the Gr. αὖ (cf. αὖτε and αὐτάρ), and with the Sanscr. vā = or, with which again may be compared ve and vel; v. Corss. Ausspr. II. p. 595, and also pp. 130, 223, 411], or; and repeated: aut... aut, either... or; so in Sanscr. vā... vā.
In gen. it puts in the place of a previous assertion another, objectively and absolutely antithetical to it, while vel indicates that the contrast rests upon subjective opinion or choice; i. e. aut is objective, vel subjective, or aut excludes one term, vel makes the two indifferent.
Used singly, or: omnia bene sunt ei dicenda, qui hoc se posse profitetur aut eloquentiae nomen relinquendum est,: quibusnam manibus aut quibus viribus,: Vinceris aut vincis,: cita mors venit aut victoria laeta,: ruminat herbas aut aliquam in magno sequitur grege, et persaep. (cf. on the contrary, : quae neque confirmare argumentis, neque refellere in animo est: ex ingenio suo quisque demat vel addat fidem).—
Repeated, aut ... aut, either... or: Ubi enim potest illa aetas aut calescere vel apricatione melius vel igni, aut vicissim umbris aquisve refrigerari salubrius?: Nam ejus per unam, ut audio, aut vivam aut moriar sententiam,; : aut, quicquid igitur eodem modo concluditur, probabitis, aut ars ista nulla est,: partem planitiae aut Jovis templum aut oppidum tenet,: terra in universum aut silvis horrida aut paludibus foeda,: hoc bellum quis umquam arbitraretur aut ab omnibus imperatoribus uno anno aut omnibus annis ab uno imperatore confici posse?.—
More than twice repeated: aut equos Alere aut canes ad venandum, aut ad philosophos, Ter And. 1, 1, 29: Uxor, si cesses, aut te amare cogitat Aut tete amare aut potare atque animo obsequi,; so four times in ; five times in ; ; and sqq.; and six times in .—
Sometimes double disjunctive phrases with aut... aut are placed together: Adsentior Crasso, ne aut de C. Laelii soceri mei aut de hujus generi aut arte aut gloriā detraham,: res ipsa et rei publicae tempus aut me ipsum, quod nolim, aut alium quempiam aut invitabit aut dehortabitur,.—
Repeated after negatives: ne aut ille alserit Aut ceciderit atque aliquid praefregerit,: ne tanti facinoris immanitas aut exstitisse aut non vindicata esse videatur,; ; ; : neque enim sunt aut obscura aut non multa post commissa,; ; ; ; : nec milites ad scelus missos aut numero validos aut animo promptos,; ; : nec erit mirabilis illic Aut Stratocles aut cum molli Demetrius Haemo,: neque aut quis esset ante detexit aut gubernatorem cedere adversae tempestati passus est,; : Nec aut Persae aut Macedones dubitavere,: Non sum aut tam inhumanus aut tam alienus a Sardis. ; : Nihil est tam aut fragile aut flexibile quam etc.,—
In interrogations: quo modo aut geometres cernere ea potest, quae aut nulla sunt aut internosci a falsis non possunt aut is, qui fidibus utitur, explere numeros et conficere versus?; so ; ; .—
In comparative clauses: talis autem simulatio vanitati est conjunctior quam aut liberalitati aut honestati,.—
Esp.
Placed singly, to connect to something more important that which is less so, or at least.
Absol.: Incute vim ventis submersasque obrue puppes, Aut age diversos et dissice corpora ponto, Rib. (furens Juno et irata, quod gravissimum credebat, optavit, deinde quod secundum intulit, P.): quaero, num injuste aut improbe fecerit,or at least unfairly,: a se postulari aut exspectari aliquid suspicantur,: quā re vi aut clam agendum est,or at least by stealth,: profecto cuncti aut magna pars Siccensium fidem mutavissent,: Audendum est aliquid universis aut omnia singulis patienda,: pars a centurionibus aut praetoriarum cohortium militibus caesi,: potentiā suā numquam aut raro ad impotentiam usus,.—
With certe, etc., v.infra, F. 2.—
To connect something which must take place, if that which is previously stated does not, or, otherwise, or else, in the contrary case, = alioqui: Redduc uxorem, aut quam obrem non opus sit cedo,: id (principium) nec nasci potest nec mori, aut concidat omne caelum etc., (Seyffert ad h. l., but preferring ut non; B. and K. and Kühner, vel): nunc manet insontem gravis exitus: aut ego veri Vana feror,: effodiuntur bulbi ante ver: aut deteriores fiunt,: Mutatione recreabitur sicut in cibis... Aut dicant iste mihi, quae sit alia ratio discendi,; .—
To restrict or correct an expression which is too general or inaccurate, or, or rather, or more accurately.
Absol.: de hominum genere, aut omnino de animalium loquor,; ; : Aut scilicet tua libertas disserendi amissa est, aut tu is es, qui in disputando non tuum judicium sequare,: cenaene causā, aut tuae mercedis gratiā Nos nostras aedīs postulas comburere? or rather, etc., .—In this signification aut sometimes begins a new clause: Potestne igitur quisquam dicere, inter eum, qui doleat, et inter eum, qui in voluptate sit, nihil interesse? Aut, ita qui sentiet, non apertissime insaniat? or is not rather, etc., : Quid est enim temeritate turpius? Aut quid tam temerarium tamque indignum sapientis gravitate atque constantiā, quam, etc.,; ; .—
With potius (v. infra, F. 4.).—
Neque ... aut sometimes, but chiefly in the poets, takes the place of neque... neque: Neque ego hanc abscondere furto Speravi, ne finge, fugam; nec conjugis umquam Praetendi taedas aut haec in foedera veni,: Si neque avaritiam neque sordes aut mala lustra Obiciet vere quisquam mihi, Bentl., but ac, K. and H.: Nunc neque te longi remeantem pompa triumphi Excipit aut sacras poscunt Capitolia lauros,: Nam neque plebeiam aut dextro sine numine cretam Servo animam,: Neque enim Tyriis Cynosura carinis Certior aut Grais Helice servanda magistris,; so also Tacitus: nec litore tenus adcrescere aut resorberi, Agr. 10; G. 7 ter; H. 1, 32; so after non: Non eo dico, quo mihi veniat in dubium tua fides, aut quo etc.,: non jure aut legibus cognoscunt,; ; ; after haud: Haud alias populus plus occultae vocis aut suspicacis silentii permisit,; after nihil: nihil caedis aut praedae,; ; .—
The poets connect by aut... vel, vel... aut, instead of aut... aut, or vel... vel: Quotiens te votui Argu

rippum Conpellare aut contrectare conloquive aut contui? : aut appone dapes, Vare, vel aufer opes, (this epigram is rejected by Schneid.): Non ars aut astus belli vel dextera deerat,.—

In connection with other particles.
Aut etiam, to complete or strengthen an assertion, or also, or even: quid ergo aut hunc prohibet, aut etiam Xenocratem, etc.,: conjectura in multas aut diversas, aut etiam in contrarias partes,; : si aut ambigue aut inconstanter aut incredibiliter dicta sunt, aut etiam aliter ab alio dicta,: etsi omnia aut scripta esse a tuis arbitror, aut etiam nuntiis ac rumore perlata,.—So with one aut: quod de illo acceperant, aut etiam suspicabantur,; : si modo sim (orator), aut etiam quicumque sim,; .—
Aut certe, aut modo, aut quidem, or aut sane, to restrict a declaration, or at least (cf. II. A.).
Aut certe: ac video hanc primam ingressionem meam aut reprehensionis aliquid, aut certe admirationis habituram,; : quo enim uno vincebamur a victā Graeciā, id aut ereptum illis est, aut certe nobis cum illis communicatum,; so Dolabella ap. ; ; ; ; ; .—
Aut modo: Si umquam posthac aut amasso Casinam, aut obcepso modo,.—
Aut quidem: Proinde desinant quidam quaerere ultra aut opinari... aut quidem vetustissimā nave impositos jubebo avehi,.—
Aut sane: Afer aut Sardus sane,.—
Aut vero, to connect a more important thought, or indeed, or truly: Quem tibi aut hominem, aut vero deum, auxilio futurum putas?: Quis enim tibi hoc concesserit, aut initio genus hominum se oppidis moenibusque saepsisse? Aut vero etc.,.—
Aut potius, for correction or greater definiteness, or rather (cf. II. C.): Erravit, aut potius insanivit Apronius?: proditores aut potius apertos hostes,: nemo est injustus, aut incauti potius habendi sunt improbi,: Quae est ergo ista ratio, aut quae potius ista amentia?.—
Aut ne... quidem: ego jam aut rem aut ne spem quidem exspecto,!*? Aut regularly precedes the words of its clause, but sometimes in the poets it takes the second place: Saturni aut sacram me tenuisse diem, Lachm.: justos aut reperire pedes,: Persequar aut studium linguae etc.,: Fer pater, inquit, opem! Tellus aut hisce, vel istam, etc., (Merk., ait): Balteus aut fluxos gemmis adstrinxit amictus,, where some read haud. See more upon this word in Hand, Turs. I. pp. 525-558.

la:verb:autumo.html:
autŭmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n.
for aitumo, as a lengthened form of aio; cf. negumo for nego; for the termination -tumo, cf. aes, aestimo, q. v., aeditumus, finitumus, and maritumus
.
Lit., to say aye, to affirm (mostly of questionable assertions, Ellis ad ; opp. nego, to say nay); hence, to assert, aver, say, name (chiefly anteclass.; esp. freq. in Plaut.; syn.: dico, affirmo, confirmo; used only once by Ter. and Hor., and never by Cic., Lucr., or Verg.): Ipsus sese ut neget esse eum qui siet, Meque ut esse autumet qui ipsus est,: factum id esse hic non negat... et deinde facturum autumat, * : flexa non falsa autumare dictio Delphis solet, Pac. ap. ; so Lucil. ib.: aut hic est aut hic affore actutum autumo,: quas (res) si autumem omnis, nimis longus sermost,; ; ; ; ; ; 5, 2, 8; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; : te esse Tiburtem autumant, * ; : ab Elissā Tyriā, quam quidam Dido autumant, Carthago conditur, Halm.—In pass.: quasi salsa muriatica esse autumantur,.—
Meton., effect for cause, to think, believe: bene quam meritam esse autumas, Dicis male mereri, auct. ap. ; (Trag. Rel. p. 265 Rib.).

a utensil for cooking (somewhat like our tea - urns): in quibus (vasis) est authepsa illa, quam tanto pretio nuper mercatus est,: argenteae,.
